newsitem.title: SPAIN: Peseta relaxes as market focus shifts to dollar.
newsitem.headline: Peseta relaxes as market focus shifts to dollar.

text.p: The peseta has relaxed into a comfortable range against the mark, where it should remain for the foreseeable future, attracting little interest as the spotlight shifts to other markets, traders said.
Anxiety over European economic and monetary union (EMU) depressed southern European markets late last week, prompting the Spanish and Italian central banks to intervene to prop up their currencies.
But by Friday, EMU fears had been brushed aside and calm was restored to the Spanish market as the dollar became the focus of traders' attentions.
"There is not much interest in the peseta at the moment and we will probably remained fixed in a 40-50 pip range for the foreseeable future," said one dealer.

Dealers said a move toward either 84 or 85 per mark would prompt the Bank of Spain to return to the market but for now the central bank seemed comfortable with current levels and had not felt the need to intervene for some days.
By 1200 GMT, the peseta was trading at 84.63/65 per mark compared with levels seen late on Thursday of 84.57/59.

"The central bank is in heaven when they see the peseta around 84.50 per mark..it's good for EMU entry and inflation pressures," one dealer said. "Only if they see 84.00 or 85.00 will they come back in."
Dealers said they would be keeping a keen eye on the dollar and U.S. payrolls data due later on Friday for signs of room for a U.S. interest rate hike.
Analysts are forecasting a rise in non-farm payrolls of 230,000 in February and a 0.4 percent rise in average hourly earnings.
Spain's labour reform talks have had little influence on the currency and dealers said they did not expect the outcome to signficantly affect the peseta.
"The market is quite relaxed and is more preoccupied by speculation over monetary union and the situation in Germany rather than talks in Spain between employers and unions," one dealer said.
Employers said they would take a break in talks until next Wednesday to consider new proposals. However, they remained optimistic that a deal would eventually be reached.
The central bank is thought to be keen to hold the peseta in the 84 to 85 per mark band in the run-up to a single European currency.
Last week it intervened heavily, buying pesetas at around 84.90, to stop the Spanish currency weakening past 85 to the mark.
Dealers said even if the Bank of Spain allowed the Spanish currency to break 85 per mark, it was unlikely to move much further past 85.25.
"The market is just not aggressive enough at the moment to shift out of the 84.50 to 85.00 per mark band," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
"Even when we had our mini meltdown last Friday, the peseta did not have the energy to move past 85.00 per mark." -- Madrid newsroom + 34 1 585 2161
